messages.subject: Using dconstraint to constrain a parameter vector
messages.subject_clean: Using dconstraint to constrain a parameter vector
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to sample while constraining a parameter of interest. I could use the T() function, but I wanted to give some probability on the constraint (If I understood the manual correctly).

Using "dconstraint" and constrain_data of 0.9 (following the example from the Nimble manual), I wanted to sample such that 90% of the time, all of the elements of the vector mu are positive; there is 10% of chance that the parameter vector could be negative. I consider that this 10%-level chance is prior from my domain knowledge.

I found that when the parameter is scalar, this works fine, but when the parameter is a vector only the first element of the vector works properly (please see the (commented out) Result below).

I wonder if my approach is a correct way of constraining a parameter vector or if there is a better way.

By the way, I switched from JAGS and am enjoying using NIMBLE although there is a lot to learn.

My test code is shown below. Please note that here I used  constrain_data of 1 to clearly show the problem.

Thank you.

- Seongeun

-------------

library (nimble)

testCode <- nimbleCode(

{

for (i in 1:10) {

mu [i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)

constraint_data ~ dconstraint( mu [i] > 0 )

}

})

Data$constraint_data  = 1

Inits = list (mu = rep (1, 10))

test <- nimbleModel(code = testCode, name = 'test',

data = Data, inits = Inits, check=FALSE)

cat ('Start compiling model\n')

Cpump <- compileNimble(test)

testConf <- configureMCMC(test, print = FALSE)

testMCMC <- buildMCMC(pumpConf)

CpumpMCMC <- compileNimble(testMCMC, project = test)

CpumpMCMC$run(10000)

samples <- as.matrix(CpumpMCMC$mvSamples)

# Result

#> apply (samples, 2, min)

#mu1[1]        mu1[2]        mu1[3]        mu1[4]        mu1[5]

#0.0003961858 -4.0777302149 -3.4941854526 -3.8758376177 -3.9843441512

#mu1[6]        mu1[7]        mu1[8]        mu1[9]       mu1[10]

#-3.7386332831 -3.7491177365 -3.4818009857 -3.6089527489 -4.1066725751

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Now I clearly understand the problem.

In the manual, it says "Formally, dconstraint(cond) is a probability distribution on {0, 1} such that P(1) = 1 if cond is TRUE and P(0) = 1 if cond is FALSE." (p. 47). I was confused by the words "probability distribution". It should be a discrete one but I misinterpreted it as a continuous on [0,1].

By specifying 0.8, I hoped that 80% of the time, the condition is true, i.e., P(1 or cond == TRUE) = 0.8 giving some uncertainty (because I am not 100% sure that P(1 or cond == TRUE) = 1).

Thanks for your clarification and help.

- Seongeun

messages.body_plain:
Hi Subhomoy,

Yes, there are a few ways you might do this.

The first is to write a user-defined distribution (see User Manual) that calls your LK function. Then you can use that distribution directly in your model code.  Since your LK is written in RcppArmadillo, you have a couple of options for calling it from the user-defined distribution.  If you can access the C++ directly, you could write a C wrapper, and call that as a nimbleExternalCall.  Then compiled nimble would directly call your compiled function.  If you need to call it from R, you could use a nimbleRcall, which allows an R function to be called from compiled nimble code.  In the latter case, there would be some overhead to get from compiled nimble code into R only for the purpose of calling back out to your compiled function, but it should work.  If LK is relatively simple and you have used RcppArmadillo for linear algebra, you might be able to re-code it directly as a nimbleFunction, which code-generates Eigen C++ instead of Armadillo.  Also note that if data_vec, param_vec and/or other arguments are large, there has unfortunately been some inefficiency in passing these arguments when used from a model, but we have a branch on github where that is resolved.  If that is an issue for you, I can point you to the right branch until we merge that improvement into a release.

An entirely separate approach would be to use the sampler_RW_llFunction or sampler_RW_llFunction_block samplers (see help(samplers)).  These use random walk Metropolis-Hastings samplers (scalar or block), but you can provide any likelihood function you want, rather than relying on model calculations.  If you want to use a different sampling method in this manner, you would have to look at the source code and see how to write your own samplers based on the same idea.

I hope that helps.  Let us know further questions.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the question, and apologies for the unclear explanation of what, exactly, the WAIC procedure is doing.  I'll give an example model and MCMC algorithm that may help to explain how the calculation changes when nodes are monitored / not monitored:

    testCode <- nimbleCode({
        mu ~ dnorm(0, 2)
        theta ~ dnorm(mu, 3)
        dataNode ~ dnorm(theta, 4)
    })

  testData <- list(dataNode = 2.1)

  testModel <- nimbleModel(code, data = testData)

Suppose we build and run an MCMC algorithm in nimble for this model.  If we only monitor the "mu" node, the WAIC algorithm will calculate log probabilities for the "dataNode" by inserting each posterior sample of "mu" into the model, simulating a value of "theta" given that posterior value of "mu", and then calculating the log probability of the dataNode given the simulated "theta".

On the other hand, if we monitor both "mu" and "theta", then the WAIC algorithm will calculate log probabilities for "dataNode" by inserting each posterior sample of "theta" into the model, and calculating the log probability of the dataNode given the posterior value of "theta".  In this case, the "theta" values are obtained directly from the MCMC algorithm, rather than simulated from the "mu" values.

In both cases, the log probabilities of the "dataNode" are then used to perform the rest of the WAIC calculations.

Of course, this model may be so simple as to not be very helpful as a demonstration (sorry if that's the case!)  If you'd like to and are able, feel free to send me your model / code and I'd be happy to check it out and see if I can give some insight into why there's such a discrepancy in your WAIC values.

Thanks!

Nick

messages.subject: Re: WAIC question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks a lot for sending along the scripts.  I checked out your model, and can give some more details on what's happening with the WAIC values.  I specifically considered the case of monitoring / not monitoring the "mu" parameter.

The WAIC in NIMBLE is calculated after an MCMC has been run, and directly uses the posterior samples located in the "mvSamples" object.    When "mu" is monitored in the MCMC algorithm, the "mvSamples" object will be populated with posterior samples of "mu" as the algorithm runs - that is, values of "mu" calculated conditional on posterior values of mu_star, eta, and r.  These 'mu' values will be used when calculating the log likelihoods of your data (equation 5 in "Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models",  Gelman, Hwang, and Vehtari, Statistics and Computing 2014).

  On the other hand, if only default monitors are used (meaning that only "B[1]"   "B[2]"   "B[3]"   "a0",     and "b0" will be monitored), then during the WAIC algorithm "mu" values will be simulated from the posterior values of these parameters.  For your model, this means that we'll take a posterior sample of the monitored top-level parameters, and first use those to simulate the next level down of stochastic nodes (e.g. mu_star, eta, r).  Then, we'll simulate "mu" values from those simulatedmu_star, eta, and r  values, and use these simulated "mu" values to calculate the log likelihood of the data "y".  In this case, the data log likelihoods that are calculated will be, on average, much lower than the likelihoods calculated using posterior samples of "mu", in turn leading to the wide difference in calculated WAIC values under these two scenarios.

The paper referenced above also gives some discussion in section 2.5 about situations where you may, or may not, want to monitor downstream nodes like "mu" when calculating the WAIC.

Let me know if you have any other questions or are getting any other strange results, thanks!

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Glenn,

I just saw something like this, so I'm pretty sure the error is occurring because an MCMC sampler such as a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler (which would be used by default on s[i, 1] and s[i, 2]) is proposing values outside the valid range.  Normally these will be rejected because their prior probability is 0 (so log probability is -Inf).  However NIMBLE still attempts to calculate dependent probabilities and in doing so it triggers the error in going outside the valid range of indices in m.  I think we should make a change in NIMBLE to avoid this, maybe by checking at every step of a sequence of model calculations if a -Inf has occurred and bailing out immediately if so.  In the meantime, here are two ways you can avoid the problem.

1. Use "control = list(reflective = TRUE)" as an argument to configureMCMC().   This will make the random-walk MH samplers respect the boundary of the relevant prior.  But it may not help if you experiment with different samplers.

2. Try the following:

SX[i] <- max(0, min(ns[1] - 0.0000001, S[i,1]))
SY[i] <- max(0, min(ns[2] - 0.0000001, S[i,2]))
pOK[i] <- m[trunc(SX[i])+1, trunc(SY[i])+1]

That builds enforcement of the range of indices for m into the model, so it should be completely general.  Invalid s[i, 1] or s[i, 2] proposals in MCMC will still be rejected due to their prior.

Let us know how it goes.

-Perry

Cc: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: Error: dynamic index out of bounds

Hi Glenn,

I just saw something like this, so I'm pretty sure the error is occurring because an MCMC sampler such as a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler (which would be used by default on s[i, 1] and s[i, 2]) is proposing values outside the valid range.  Normally these will be rejected because their prior probability is 0 (so log probability is -Inf).  However NIMBLE still attempts to calculate dependent probabilities and in doing so it triggers the error in going outside the valid range of indices in m.  I think we should make a change in NIMBLE to avoid this, maybe by checking at every step of a sequence of model calculations if a -Inf has occurred and bailing out immediately if so.  In the meantime, here are two ways you can avoid the problem.

1. Use "control = list(reflective = TRUE)" as an argument to configureMCMC().   This will make the random-walk MH samplers respect the boundary of the relevant prior.  But it may not help if you experiment with different samplers.

2. Try the following:

SX[i] <- max(0, min(ns[1] - 0.0000001, S[i,1]))
SY[i] <- max(0, min(ns[2] - 0.0000001, S[i,2]))
pOK[i] <- m[trunc(SX[i])+1, trunc(SY[i])+1]

That builds enforcement of the range of indices for m into the model, so it should be completely general.  Invalid s[i, 1] or s[i, 2] proposals in MCMC will still be rejected due to their prior.

Let us know how it goes.

-Perry

>
> The WAIC in NIMBLE is calculated after an MCMC has been run, and directly uses the posterior samples located in the "mvSamples" object.    When "mu" is monitored in the MCMC algorithm, the "mvSamples" object will be populated with posterior samples of "mu" as the algorithm runs - that is, values of "mu" calculated conditional on posterior values of mu_star, eta, and r.  These 'mu' values will be used when calculating the log likelihoods of your data (equation 5 in "Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models",  Gelman, Hwang, and Vehtari, Statistics and Computing 2014).
>
>   On the other hand, if only default monitors are used (meaning that only "B[1]"   "B[2]"   "B[3]"   "a0",     and "b0" will be monitored), then during the WAIC algorithm "mu" values will be simulated from the posterior values of these parameters.  For your model, this means that we'll take a posterior sample of the monitored top-level parameters, and first use those to simulate the next level down of stochastic nodes (e.g. mu_star, eta, r).  Then, we'll simulate "mu" values from those simulatedmu_star, eta, and r  values, and use these simulated "mu" values to calculate the log likelihood of the data "y".  In this case, the data log likelihoods that are calculated will be, on average, much lower than the likelihoods calculated using posterior samples of "mu", in turn leading to the wide difference in calculated WAIC values under these two scenarios.

Apologies, Kori.  This error is related to recent changes to the RW_block sampler, which allow for saving the adaptation parameters through the course of a run (for diagnostic purposes), but instead has resulted in some errors in your case.

I've just made some changes on our development branch of NIMBLE, to this problem.  Until the next release, which will include these fixes, you can install from our development branch using:

remove.packages('nimble')
library(devtools)
install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

This should solve the problem you're having, with using the RW_block sampler when Q > 10.
